newsitem.title: CHINA: Banking moves to facilitate HK's property aims.
newsitem.headline: Banking moves to facilitate HK's property aims.

text.p: Hong Kong's hopes of capping rising property prices while boosting home ownership will depend largely on the success of its Mortgage Corporation and a drive towards mortgage securitisation, analysts said on Tuesday.
Home prices have surged beyond affordable levels here, prompting a pledge by Hong Kong's new government last week that it will increase housing supply and bolster home ownership.

But the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), Hong Kong's de facto central bank, has also voiced concerns about the rapid rise in mortgage lending and has suggested banks reduce their exposure to the property market.

"They are conflicting objectives, and securitisations and the Mortgage Corporation will provide an avenue to reconcile the two conflicting interests," said Alan Hutcheson, banking analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

The Mortgage Corp is due to become operational in the fourth quarter of this year, offering banks a chance to sell some of their mortgages to the corporation to reduce the amount of mortgage loans on their books.
Some banks have already started to move in that direction, selling some of their mortgage books in securitisation deals.

Last month, Dah Sing Bank Ltd bundled up 20 percent of its mortgage book in a US$300 million cross-border securitisation and Sanwa Finance Hong Kong Ltd completed a US$144 million cross-border securitisation.
Hong Kong Telecommunications Ltd also securitised HK$800 million of staff housing mortgages in May.

"It does help the banks continue lending to mortgage customers while keeping the Monetary Authority relatively happy in terms of high mortgage and high property-lending concentration," said Hutcheson.
Over time banks could become just mortgage originators, transferring loans to the Mortgage Corporation, while securitisations are set to become more popular, analysts said.
"I think it is a key component to the success of the government's housing policy," said Roy Ramos, regional banking analyst at Goldman Sachs.

He said the government's plans to increase overall housing supply to not less than 85,000 flats a year and achieve a home ownership rate of 70 percent in 10 years would boost demand for funds beyond the capacity of the banking system.

"Given the emerging policy on housing -- raising home ownership and increasing supply -- there is obviously going to be more demand for funds. Our view is that mortgage credit demand could easily grow by about 18 percent each year," Ramos said.
"The growth in mortgage and real estate credit will exceed the overall growth rate of the banking system so over time property exposure will increase," he said.

Despite the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's alarm at rising property exposure, analysts said they were not particularly concerned since securitisation and the Mortgage Corporation would allow banks to offload some of their exposure.
Mortgage lending also remained a major source of growth for banks and was less risky than unsecured credit activity.
"Defaults on mortgages since the early 80s has been zero - you could almost call it risk-free," said Steven Thompson, chief analyst at Nikko Securities.
Specific details on the government's housing plans, expected during a policy statement in October, should not include restrictions on bank lending, analysts predicted.

"I don't believe the Monetary Authority will want to use that route," said Raymond Lee, a banking analyst at Lehman Brothers. "My view is that the government will try to alter the supply equation for the housing market and increase supply."
